name: Money in the Family: Banking and Business Dynasties
description: The Medici, Fuggers, Rothschilds, Rockefellers, Tatas, Mitsui and others: families whose banks and firms lent to kings, built industries, passed between generations and sometimes collapsed.

checkpoints.name: Florentine bankers
checkpoints.note: The Medici Bank, founded in 1397, made the House of Medici rich enough to rule Florence and later to give the Church popes, though the bank itself failed in the 1490s.

checkpoints.name: Lenders to kings
checkpoints.note: Jakob Fugger of Augsburg lent an emperor's family the money to buy an imperial election and became one of the richest men in Europe. In Japan the Mitsui family opened a cloth shop in Edo in 1673 and later a money exchange, in 1762 the Baring family's merchant house began in London, and in Frankfurt Mayer Amschel Rothschild built the family bank.

checkpoints.name: Houses across borders
checkpoints.note: Rothschild's five sons opened banks in Frankfurt, London, Paris, Vienna and Naples. In Germany the Krupp steelworks and the Siemens electrical firm grew into family-run industrial giants, the Lehman brothers began as cotton traders in Alabama, and in India Jamsetji Tata began trading in 1868.

checkpoints.name: Gilded dynasties
checkpoints.note: John D. Rockefeller's oil fortune founded a dynasty of bankers, politicians and givers, and J. P. Morgan's bank steadied American finance in the panic of 1907. William Randolph Hearst turned an inherited mining fortune into a newspaper empire, and Nintendo began in 1889 as the Yamauchi family's playing-card shop.

checkpoints.name: Survival and collapse
checkpoints.note: The Ford family kept control of its motor company, the Toyoda family founded Toyota, the Lee family built Samsung, and the Oppenheimers ran De Beers for most of the century, while Ratan Tata took the Tata Group abroad. Others fell: Barings collapsed in 1995, Krupp merged away in 1999 and Lehman Brothers failed in 2008.
